subject: The World Around Us
title: Karan's Invisible Adventure
hook: Karan and his sister Meera discover the invisible air that surrounds them and does amazing things.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: Karan's sister who experiments with air

slides.title: Air Around Us
slides.storyContext: Karan sits by his window and watches the wind blow the leaves. He wonders: 'What makes the leaves move? I can't see it, but something is there.'

slides.title: The Invisible Friend
slides.storyContext: One afternoon, Karan and Meera play with a kite in the park near their Mumbai apartment. The kite flies high and dances in the sky. 'What's making it fly?' asks Meera. Karan thinks hard. His teacher uncle, who is sitting nearby, hears the question and smiles. 'That's air! It's all around you, but you can't see it. Air makes the kite fly, moves your hair, and fills your lungs when you breathe!'

slides.title: What Is Air?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle brings Karan and Meera to a quiet spot under a big tree. 'Air is invisible,' he says, 'but it is real and it is everywhere. Even though you can't see it, you feel it, you breathe it, and you need it to live.'

points.text: Air is all around us - outside and inside buildings
Air takes up space - even when you can't see it
Air is made of many tiny invisible parts mixed together (gases)

slides.inSimpleWords: Air is invisible, but it's real and everywhere around you.

image.alt: What Is Air? — Air Around Us

slides.title: Karan's Wind Discovery
slides.storyContext: That evening, Karan sits on the balcony and feels a cool breeze on his face. 'This is air!' he says to Meera. 'I can feel it but not see it. Meera, wave this sheet - I want to see if air can move it.' Meera waves the white sheet high, and it flutters and moves beautifully. 'See? Air is moving the sheet. Air must be very strong even though we can't see it.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Air moves things - you can see what air does even though you cannot see air itself.

slides.title: We Breathe Air
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle asks the children to take a deep breath. 'Did you feel something? That's you breathing air! Your body needs air to live and play.' He shows them a picture of lungs inside the human body. 'When you breathe, air goes into your lungs, and your body uses a special part of air called oxygen to stay alive.'

points.text: Breathing means taking air into your lungs and letting it out
Your body needs oxygen from the air to work and play
Every living animal - dogs, birds, fish, insects - needs air to breathe (or water with air in it)

slides.inSimpleWords: Your lungs drink air so your body can grow strong and play.

image.alt: We Breathe Air — Air Around Us

slides.title: The Breathing Experiment
slides.storyContext: Meera puts her hand on her chest and takes a deep breath. 'My chest moves up when I breathe in!' she notices. Teacher Uncle nods: 'That's your lungs filling with air. When you breathe out, your chest goes down. This happens about 20,000 times a day without you even thinking about it!'

example.problem: Put your hand on your chest and breathe in deeply. What do you feel?
example.solution: Your chest rises when you breathe in - that is your lungs filling with air. When you breathe out, your chest falls. Your lungs are like two sponges that fill with air and push it out, bringing oxygen to your whole body.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your lungs are like sponges that suck in air and push it out.

slides.title: Air Moves Things
slides.storyContext: Meera runs with her kite and feels the wind push on her face. Karan watches leaves flying off a tree during the breeze. 'Air is moving things!' says Karan. Teacher Uncle nods: 'Moving air is wind. Wind can do many jobs - it pushes kites, dries clothes on a clothesline, turns windmills, and even helps sail-boats move across the water.'

points.text: Moving air is called wind
Wind pushes light things like leaves, kites, and dust
Wind can be gentle (a soft breeze) or very strong (a storm)

slides.inSimpleWords: Wind is air that moves - it pushes things and makes them fly.

slides.title: The Windy Day
slides.storyContext: One afternoon, a strong wind blows through the park. Karan sees leaves swirling, dust flying up, and everyone's hair blowing wildly. A vendor's hat flies off! 'Look how much air can do!' says Karan to his sister. Teacher Uncle explains: 'This is a strong wind. Wind is created when air moves from one place to another. The more air moves, the stronger the wind becomes.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Strong wind is fast-moving air - it can push and move many things at once.

slides.title: Air Takes Up Space
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle shows Karan a balloon. 'Watch,' he says, and blows it up. The balloon gets bigger and bigger, filled with air from his mouth. Then he shows Meera a plastic bag and waves it through the air. 'The bag is catching invisible air - you can see the air by the bump in the bag!'

points.text: You can feel air by waving something - like a fan or a piece of paper
You can see air's effects - a flag fluttering, dust floating, hair blowing
You can trap air in a balloon or bag to prove it takes up space

slides.inSimpleWords: Even though you cannot see air, you can feel it and see what it does.

slides.title: The Cup and Water Experiment
slides.storyContext: Karan and Meera do a fun experiment. Karan takes a plastic cup and pushes it down into a bucket of water upside-down. The cup stays dry inside! 'How?' asks Meera. 'Air was in the cup, and air took up space,' explains Teacher Uncle. 'The air kept the water out!'

example.problem: Push an upside-down cup into water. What happens to the paper napkin inside the cup?
example.solution: The napkin stays dry! Air in the cup takes up space and prevents water from entering. This proves air is real and takes up space, even though you cannot see it.

slides.title: Plants Make Air For Us
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle points to the big tree above them. 'This tree is special. It takes air from the sky and changes it. The tree gives us oxygen - the good air we breathe. And it takes the air we breathe out (carbon dioxide) and uses it to grow bigger!'

points.text: Trees and plants make oxygen that we breathe
We breathe out carbon dioxide, and plants use it to grow
Plants and people help each other - we need their oxygen, they need our carbon dioxide

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants are air-makers - they give us the clean air we need to breathe.

image.alt: Plants Make Air For Us — Air Around Us

slides.title: Meera's Plant Mystery
slides.storyContext: Meera notices that in the morning, leaves have water droplets on them even though it didn't rain. She asks Teacher Uncle. 'That's water from the plant,' he explains. 'Plants breathe too! They take in air from the sky and release some water and air back out. That water that you see is part of how plants help make the air we breathe.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Plants release water and air - they help keep our air clean and fresh.

slides.title: Different Types of Air Movement
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle teaches Karan and Meera about different kinds of air movement. 'Sometimes air moves gently - like a cool breeze on a warm day. Sometimes it moves fast and strong - like a storm wind. And sometimes air just sits still, filling a space quietly.'

points.text: Breeze - gentle, cool air movement that feels nice on your skin
Wind - stronger air movement that can push things and blow dust
Storm - very strong, fast wind that can knock things over
Still air - air that is not moving, but still fills the space around you

slides.inSimpleWords: Air can move gently like a breeze, or fast like wind, or stay still.

slides.title: Air Pressure Experiment
slides.storyContext: Karan tries another experiment at school. He takes a bottle and puts a balloon over the opening. He sucks air out of the bottle through a straw. The balloon gets sucked inside the bottle! 'What happened?' he asks Teacher Uncle. 'There's less air in the bottle now, so the air outside pushes the balloon in. This is called air pressure.'

example.problem: Put a balloon over a bottle opening. Suck air out of the bottle through a straw. What happens to the balloon?
example.solution: The balloon gets sucked into the bottle! This happens because there is less air pressure inside the bottle than outside. The air outside is heavier and pushes the balloon inward.

slides.inSimpleWords: Air pushes in all directions - this pushing is called air pressure.

slides.title: Karan's Invisible Discovery
slides.storyContext: That night, Karan thinks about everything he learned. He realizes air is everywhere - in his room, in his lungs, in the clouds, even in water. He tries to count all the places air is. 'Air is in the sky, in the ground, in my body, in the ocean water... air is everywhere!' He feels amazed that something invisible is so important.
slides.inSimpleWords: Air is the most important invisible thing on Earth - it is everywhere.

slides.title: Air and Health
slides.storyContext: At school, the teacher talks about clean air. 'Some air is clean - like fresh air from trees. Some air is dirty - like smoke from cars or factories. Breathing clean air is very important for your health.'

points.text: Fresh air from nature is clean and good for your lungs
Pollution - dirty air from cars, factories, and smoke - can hurt your health
Plants help clean the air by taking in bad gases and making good oxygen
It's important to spend time outside where the air is fresher and cleaner

slides.inSimpleWords: Clean air from nature is healthy - dirty air from pollution can hurt you.

slides.title: Air Detectives Challenge
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle asks: 'Today, find 5 ways you can SEE air, even though air is invisible. Hunt around your home and garden.'

example.problem: Find 5 examples of things that show air is real and around us.
example.solution: 1) Blow on a paper - it moves. 2) Watch smoke rise - air carries it. 3) Feel wind on your face. 4) See leaves fall - air plays with them. 5) Blow a balloon - air fills it and it gets bigger. 6) See a flag fluttering. 7) Watch water ripple when you blow on it. 8) See dust floating in sunlight.

slides.title: Air Usage Tracking
slides.storyContext: Meera makes a list of all the ways air helps her every day. She realizes she uses air so much that she never even thinks about it. Air is helping her right now, she laughs.

example.problem: List 10 ways air helps you or people around you every day.
example.solution: 1. Breathing (life) 2. Cooling with fans 3. Flying kites 4. Drying clothes 5. Helping birds fly 6. Carrying sounds 7. Growing plants (CO2) 8. Sailing boats 9. Turning windmills 10. Blowing bubbles. 11. Blowing out candles 12. Singing (moving vocal cords) 13. Running fast (more air needed) 14. Playing sports (wind resistance)

slides.inSimpleWords: Air helps us breathe, play, cool down, and do thousands of daily tasks.

slides.title: When Air Is Missing
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle shows Karan and Meera a video of astronauts in space. Without a space suit and air, they cannot breathe. The space suit brings air to them from a tank. In the mountains where the air is very thin, some climbers feel dizzy and weak. This shows how important air is to us.
slides.inSimpleWords: Life needs air - without it, even astronauts cannot survive.

slides.title: Air in Different Places
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle asks the children: Where is there air? Karan and Meera think. In the sky, in caves, in water, inside our bodies, inside buildings. Yes, air is everywhere, says Teacher Uncle. Even under the ground in soil pockets. Air surrounds everything on Earth.

points.text: Air is in the sky and atmosphere high above us
Air is in caves, buildings, and enclosed spaces
Air is mixed in water - fish breathe this air through their gills
Air is in soil - roots use this air to grow strong

slides.inSimpleWords: Air is everywhere on Earth - in sky, water, soil, and indoor spaces.

slides.title: Air Helps Us Play Sports
slides.storyContext: Karan and Meera notice that when they run, they need more air. Their breathing gets faster and deeper. When they play cricket or badminton, they feel the wind of the ball moving through air. Even sports depend on air! Air makes the ball move, it fills their lungs, and it cools them down when they sweat.
slides.inSimpleWords: Sports depend on air - running needs more air, balls fly through air.

slides.title: Sound Travels in Air
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle plays a sound experiment. He rings a bell inside a glass jar with air. You can hear the sound. Then he uses a pump to remove the air from the jar. Ring the bell again! No sound comes out! This proves that sound needs air to travel.

points.text: Sound travels as waves through air
Without air, you cannot hear sounds
Sound travels slower than light - that is why you see lightning before you hear thunder
Loud sounds need more air movement - soft sounds need less

slides.inSimpleWords: Sound waves travel through air - without air, there is no sound.

slides.title: Design Your Own Air Experiment
slides.storyContext: Teacher Uncle challenges the children: You learned about air taking space and air pressure. Now design your own experiment to show something about air. What materials will you use? What will you measure?

example.problem: Design an experiment to prove air is all around us.
example.solution: Examples: (1) Put a bottle in water upside-down and see if air stays inside. (2) Blow a balloon and measure how big it gets. (3) Use a paper fan to feel air movement. (4) Pour water while tilting a cup and watch air bubbles escape. (5) Blow through a straw into water and watch bubbles.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can design your own air experiment using simple things at home.

slides.title: What We Learned About Air
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Karan flies his kite one more time. Now he understands the invisible force helping it soar. He takes a deep breath and smiles at his sister.

points.text: Air is invisible but real - it surrounds us everywhere
We breathe air to get oxygen that keeps us alive
Wind is moving air that pushes light things
You can prove air is real by feeling it and seeing what it does
Plants give us clean air - we should take care of trees
Air has pressure - it pushes in all directions
Clean air is important for our health and happiness

slides.inSimpleWords: Air is invisible, but you breathe it, feel it, and see it move things.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Learn to Stay Safe
hook: Ravi and Priya discover important safety rules that keep them and their friends safe every day.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: smart girl who asks safety questions

slides.title: Safety Rules
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya play together at their school in Bangalore. One day, Ravi almost gets hurt when he runs near the stairs. His parent explains why safety rules are important.

slides.title: A Scary Moment
slides.storyContext: During lunch break, Ravi runs fast toward the playground stairs. His friend Priya shouts: 'Stop! That's dangerous!' Ravi nearly slips and falls. His heart beats fast. At home, his parent sits with him and Priya and says: 'Safety rules are not to spoil fun - they are to keep you healthy and happy. Let me show you the rules that matter most.'

slides.title: Safety at Home: Kitchen and Stove
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother is cooking lunch in the kitchen. Priya asks: 'Can I help cook?' Her mother smiles and nods. 'Yes! But first, these are the kitchen safety rules. Listen carefully so you do not get burned.'

points.text: Never touch the stove, oven, or hot pans - they can burn your skin badly
Always keep your hands away from the cooking fire or gas flame
Never play with sharp knives - ask an adult to cut things
Keep water and other things away from electrical outlets

slides.inSimpleWords: The kitchen has hot things and sharp things - stay safe by asking an adult before touching anything.

image.alt: Safety at Home: Kitchen and Stove — Safety Rules

slides.title: Priya Learns Hot vs Cold
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother shows her two pots - one has steam rising from it, and one is empty. 'This one is hot,' she says, pointing. 'Never touch it even if you think it is cool. Hot things stay hot for a long time and can give you a bad burn. A burn can hurt for days and leave a mark on your skin.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Hot pots and pans stay hot even when they stop cooking - never touch them.

slides.title: Safety at Home: Stairs and Falls
slides.storyContext: Ravi remembers his near-fall on the stairs. His parent says: 'That could have hurt you badly. Let's talk about stair safety. Ravi remembers learning about this in his safety class at school.'

points.text: Always hold the railing when going up or down stairs
Do not run, jump, or play on stairs - walk slowly and carefully
Do not carry things that hide what's ahead when going down stairs
Keep toys and bags off the stairs so nobody trips

slides.inSimpleWords: Stairs are tricky - hold the railing, go slow, and watch your step.

image.alt: Safety at Home: Stairs and Falls — Safety Rules

slides.title: Safe vs Unsafe Stair Use
slides.storyContext: Ravi's parent shows him what NOT to do on stairs: running, jumping, carrying big boxes, not holding the railing. Then she shows SAFE ways: walking step-by-step, holding the rail, keeping eyes on steps, moving slowly.

example.problem: What are 3 dangerous things to do on stairs?
example.solution: 1. Running on stairs - you can slip and fall badly. 2. Carrying large boxes that hide steps - you cannot see where to step. 3. Not holding the railing - you have nothing to catch you if you fall. SAFE: Walk slowly, hold the railing, watch each step carefully.

slides.inSimpleWords: Walking carefully and holding the railing keeps you safe from falls.

slides.title: Safety on the Street and Road
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya's parent takes them for a walk near their apartment in Pune. They reach a busy road. Cars and auto-rickshaws rush past. 'Now watch,' says their parent. 'This is where many accidents happen. You must follow road safety rules.'

points.text: Always hold an adult's hand when crossing a road - never run across alone
Look both ways (left, right, left again) before crossing
Cross only at a zebra crossing or traffic signal if one is near
Wear bright clothes or a reflective vest so drivers can see you in the dark

slides.inSimpleWords: Roads are dangerous - hold an adult's hand, look both ways, and cross when it is safe.

slides.title: Ravi Almost Gets Hit
slides.storyContext: On their walk, Ravi sees a friend across the road and wants to run over. His parent holds his hand firmly and says: 'Stop! See that car coming fast? If you had run, that car could have hit you. Always wait for an adult and cross at the safe place.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Cars go very fast and can hurt you - never cross a road alone.

slides.title: Safety at School: Playgrounds
slides.storyContext: At school the next day, Priya's teacher talks about playground safety during assembly. 'Playgrounds are fun,' she says, 'but we must follow rules so everyone stays happy and healthy.'

points.text: Take turns on slides, swings, and seesaws - do not rush or push
Wear shoes with good grip to avoid slipping
If someone is on the slide, wait at the bottom - do not go down if they're coming up
Tell an adult if you get hurt or if you see something dangerous

slides.inSimpleWords: Playgrounds are safe when everyone takes turns and follows the rules.

slides.title: Playground Safety Quiz
slides.storyContext: Priya's teacher gives the class a game where she describes playground situations and children say SAFE or UNSAFE.

example.problem: You are waiting to go on the swing. Another child says they will push you really high. Is this safe?
example.solution: UNSAFE - do not let anyone push you on a swing. Ask a teacher if you want to use the swing. Pushing can make you fall off.

slides.inSimpleWords: Only adults should help with swings - other children pushing can be dangerous.

slides.title: Safety With Strangers
slides.storyContext: Ravi's parent has a serious talk with him and Priya. 'I need to teach you something very important. Some people may try to hurt children. You need to know what to do and what NOT to do.'

points.text: Never go with a stranger, even if they offer candy or gifts
If a stranger touches you in a way that feels bad, say NO loudly and run to find an adult
Tell your parent, teacher, or another trusted adult about anyone who makes you feel scared or uncomfortable
Safe adults include: parents, teachers, police, doctors, and people your parents tell you are safe

slides.inSimpleWords: Strangers can be unsafe. Stay close to your parents and tell them if something feels wrong.

slides.title: Priya Practices Saying No
slides.storyContext: After the talk, Priya practices saying NO loudly with her parent. 'No! I do not want this!' She practices running away from her parent to practice what she would do. Her parent says: 'Good! That is how you should act. Your body is yours, and you have the right to say no to anything that feels wrong.'
slides.inSimpleWords: You can always say NO to any adult who makes you feel unsafe.

slides.title: Safety With Electricity and Water
slides.storyContext: Ravi's parent teaches him about electrical safety: 'Electricity is very dangerous. It can hurt or even kill you. Never play with electrical outlets, plugs, or wires.'

points.text: Never put fingers, toys, or anything into electrical outlets
Never touch plugs or cords with wet hands
Keep water far away from electrical things like fans, lights, and chargers
If you see a broken or burning electrical thing, tell an adult right away

slides.inSimpleWords: Electricity and water together are very dangerous - keep them apart.

slides.title: Safety at Home: What Would You Do?
slides.storyContext: Ravi's parent shows him different home safety situations and asks: 'What is the safe choice?'

example.problem: You are home alone in the kitchen. You see a pot of boiling water on the stove and feel very hungry. Do you: (A) carefully pick up the pot to make noodles, (B) wait for your parent to come home or call them for help?
example.solution: CHOICE B is safe. Never touch hot pots, pans, or stove flames. Always ask an adult to cook for you or to help you. A burn can hurt you badly and take a long time to heal.

slides.title: Safety With Bicycles and Scooters
slides.storyContext: Ravi gets a new bicycle and is very excited. But his parent says: 'Before you ride, we need to learn bike safety. A bicycle accident can hurt you badly.'

points.text: Always wear a helmet - it protects your head if you fall
Check your brakes before riding - they must work properly
Ride on paths or roads meant for bicycles, not on busy streets alone
Wear bright colors so cars and people can see you

slides.inSimpleWords: Helmets save lives - always wear one when riding a bicycle or scooter.

slides.title: Safety Detective Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya's teacher gives the class a fun challenge: 'Find 5 safety rules being followed at home or school today. Tell your friend why each rule is important.'

example.problem: Walk around your home or school and point out 5 things people do to stay safe. Why is each rule important?
example.solution: Examples: (1) Railing on stairs - prevents falls. (2) Light switches away from water taps - stops electric shock. (3) No running near stairs - avoids tripping and falling. (4) Holding parent's hand on the street - keeps you from running into traffic. (5) Keeping toys off the floor - stops people tripping. (6) Using a seatbelt in a car - protects you in a crash.

slides.title: My Safety Plan
slides.storyContext: Priya's teacher gives everyone homework: 'Make a safety plan for your home. Write or draw the safest way to: (1) Go up and down stairs, (2) Cross a street, (3) Escape if there is a fire, (4) Call for help if you need it.'

example.problem: Create a safety plan for your home and neighborhood.
example.solution: STAIRS: Hold railing, step slowly. STREET: Hold parent's hand, look both ways, use crossing. FIRE: Know where the exit is, call 999 or go to nearest adult. HELP: Know your parent's phone number, know trusted adults nearby, know where to find a police officer or shopkeeper.

slides.inSimpleWords: Know your safety plan - it can save your life in an emergency.

slides.title: Teaching Others
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya decide to teach their younger cousin about safety. They act out different scenarios - holding the railing while going down stairs, looking both ways before crossing, saying no to strangers. Their cousin watches and learns. Being safe is cool, their cousin says.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you follow safety rules, you can teach others and help keep everyone safe.

slides.title: First Aid: What To Do If Someone Gets Hurt
slides.storyContext: At school, the nurse teaches Ravi and Priya basic first aid. If someone gets hurt, what should you do? First, tell an adult. Then, the adult can help.

points.text: Stay calm when someone gets hurt - do not panic
Do not move an injured person unless they are in danger
Tell an adult immediately - call for a teacher or parent
The adult will know what to do to help - they can call a doctor if needed

slides.inSimpleWords: If someone is hurt, stay calm and tell an adult immediately.

slides.title: First Aid Response
slides.storyContext: Your friend falls off the swing and scrapes their knee. Blood is coming. What do you do? Ravi learns the steps: Stay calm, do not move them, tell an adult, the adult will help.

example.problem: Your friend falls off the swing and scrapes their knee. Blood is coming. What do you do?
example.solution: 1. Stay calm. 2. Do not move your friend unless they are in danger. 3. Tell an adult immediately. 4. The adult will clean the wound, put a bandage on it, or call the doctor if it is serious. Never try to help on your own if the injury looks bad.

slides.inSimpleWords: When someone is hurt, stay calm and get an adult to help.

slides.title: When Priya Felt Scared
slides.storyContext: One day, an older child at school talks to Priya and makes her feel uncomfortable. She feels scared but does not know what to do. She remembers what her parent taught her and tells a teacher. The teacher talks to the older child and tells Priya she did the right thing. I am proud of you for telling an adult, says the teacher.
slides.inSimpleWords: If anyone makes you feel unsafe, always tell a trusted adult.

slides.title: Fire Safety at Home
slides.storyContext: Ravi's parent teaches him about fire safety. A fire can start from a cooking accident, candles, or faulty wires. Knowing what to do can save your life.

points.text: Know where the nearest exit is from your bedroom
If you see fire or smoke, do not try to fight it - leave immediately
Call for an adult or go outside and call 101 (fire brigade)
Never hide under a bed or in a closet during a fire - go outside

slides.inSimpleWords: In a fire, get out of the house and call for help - never hide.

slides.title: Ravi's Safety Success
slides.storyContext: A few weeks later, Ravi sees his friend playing dangerously near a window. He remembers the safety rules and tells his friend: That is unsafe! Come down carefully while holding the railing. His friend listens, and both children stay safe. Ravi feels proud that he helped keep his friend safe.
slides.inSimpleWords: Knowing safety rules helps you protect yourself and your friends.

slides.title: Water Safety
slides.storyContext: Priya's parent takes her to a swimming pool. Before she goes in the water, her parent explains water safety. Water can be fun and healthy, but it can also be dangerous. You must know how to swim and follow water safety rules.

points.text: Never go near water alone - always have an adult with you
Learn to swim at a proper swimming class, not by yourself
Wear a life jacket if you are not a good swimmer
Do not run or play roughly near water - you could slip and fall

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is fun but dangerous - always have an adult and follow water safety rules.

slides.title: Important Safety Rules to Remember
slides.storyContext: At the end of the week, Ravi and Priya make a safety poster for their bedroom. They write and draw all the rules they learned.

points.text: At home: Stay away from hot stoves, use stairs carefully, do not touch sharp things alone
On the street: Hold an adult's hand, look both ways, cross at safe spots
At school: Take turns, play carefully, tell an adult if hurt
With people: Only go with trusted adults, tell an adult if someone makes you uncomfortable
Safety rules keep you and your friends happy and healthy
Wearing helmets and safety gear can save your life
Always tell a trusted adult if you feel scared or unsafe

slides.inSimpleWords: Follow safety rules at home, school, and outside to stay safe and healthy.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Arjun's Year of Changes
hook: Arjun watches his town change through four seasons and discovers why weather and nature change so much.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: observant boy tracking seasons through the year

characters.name: Niti
characters.role: Arjun's friend who notices seasonal changes

slides.title: Seasons
slides.storyContext: Arjun lives in Delhi. Every few months, he notices that the weather, the trees, and the way people dress all change. Why does everything keep changing?

slides.title: A Year of Change
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at a photo from January - he is wearing a thick coat and a woolly hat. Then he looks at another photo from May - he is wearing a light shirt and a hat to keep the sun away. Another photo from September shows him wearing a sweater because it is cool and rainy. In December, he is bundled up again in winter clothes. I have changed my clothes four times already this year, laughs Arjun. His gardener uncle nods: Your town has four seasons. Each season brings different weather and different clothes. Let me tell you about each one.

slides.title: Summer: The Hot Season
slides.storyContext: Niti runs toward Arjun on a hot April afternoon in Delhi. She is sweating. It is so hot! she complains. The sun is very strong. Everything is dry and hot. This is summer, says Gardener Uncle. In summer, the sun is heat is strongest. People wear light clothes and drink lots of water.

points.text: Summer is hot and dry in most of India (March to June)
The sun is strong and high in the sky - it heats up the ground, buildings, and water
People wear light clothes like t-shirts, shorts, and sandals
In summer, plants need lots of water or they will dry up

slides.inSimpleWords: Summer is hot and dry - the sun is very strong and bright.

slides.title: The Hot Summer Adventure
slides.storyContext: During the peak of summer heat in June, Arjun and Niti spend most afternoons indoors under fans and air conditioners. Even the water from the tap feels warm. The street melts a little bit. People carry umbrellas not for rain but for shade. Ice cream shops are very busy. Gardener Uncle brings them cold lemonade: This is how we stay cool and healthy in summer.
slides.inSimpleWords: Summer is so hot that we need to drink lots of water and stay in cool places.

slides.title: Monsoon: The Rainy Season
slides.storyContext: By July, dark clouds fill the sky. The monsoon has arrived. Rain pours down all day long. Arjun and Niti splash in puddles outside Arjun's house in Mumbai. Look at all this water! says Niti. This rain fills rivers, lakes, and underground water tanks, explains Gardener Uncle. It is very important for farmers and for plants to grow.

points.text: Monsoon is the rainy season (June to September) when lots of rain falls
Heavy rain cools down the air and fills water sources
Farmers plant rice and other crops just before the monsoon starts
During monsoon, the weather is cool and wet, and people wear raincoats

slides.inSimpleWords: Monsoon is rainy season - lots of water falls from the sky.

slides.title: The Monsoon Story
slides.storyContext: Niti keeps a rain journal during monsoon. She draws the number of rainy days, the puddles she jumps in, the frogs she hears croaking, and the new green growth on plants. By the end of monsoon, her journal is full of water drops and green pictures.

example.problem: What happens to plants and animals during monsoon?
example.solution: Plants drink lots of water and grow faster and greener. Frogs come out to sing and lay eggs. Farmers plant crops. Rivers and lakes fill up. Animals drink plenty of water. Everything comes alive because of the water.

slides.inSimpleWords: Monsoon rains make everything green and alive - plants love the water.

slides.title: Autumn: The Cool Season
slides.storyContext: By October, the rain stops. The weather becomes cool and pleasant. Arjun notices the leaves on trees turning yellow and orange. Some fall to the ground. The leaves are changing color! he points out. This is autumn, says Gardener Uncle. The weather becomes cooler, the sky is usually clear, and plants get ready for the cold months ahead.

points.text: Autumn is cool and dry (September to November)
Many leaves turn yellow, orange, and red before falling off trees
The weather is pleasant - not too hot and not too cold
Farmers harvest their crops that have grown strong in monsoon and autumn

slides.inSimpleWords: Autumn is cool and colorful - leaves change and harvest time comes.

slides.title: Niti's Leaf Collection
slides.storyContext: During autumn, Niti collects fallen leaves of different colors. She presses them in a book to keep them. Red, yellow, orange, brown, she counts them. Each leaf is different, just like each person is different. Gardener Uncle explains: When leaves fall, the tree is saying goodbye to them and preparing to rest in winter.
slides.inSimpleWords: Falling leaves are beautiful - they show the season is changing.

slides.title: Winter: The Cold Season
slides.storyContext: December arrives and Arjun sees his breath like a small white cloud when he goes outside on a cold morning in Bangalore. He wraps himself in a blanket. Why is it so cold? he asks, shivering. This is winter - the coldest season, explains Gardener Uncle. The sun is far away in the sky, so it does not heat the earth as much.

points.text: Winter is cold (December to February) - it is the coldest season in India
The sun is low in the sky and does not warm the earth as much
People wear warm clothes like sweaters, jackets, and hats
In some parts of northern India, water freezes and snow falls in the mountains

slides.inSimpleWords: Winter is cold - the sun is far away and does not heat the earth much.

slides.title: The Winter Morning Frost
slides.storyContext: One winter morning, Arjun wakes up and sees the grass covered in a white layer. Frost, says his mother. It is frozen water that formed when the temperature dropped very low during the night. Arjun touches the frost - it is cold and wet. By the time the sun rises, it melts and goes away. This happens in winter when it is very cold.
slides.inSimpleWords: Frost is frozen water that appears on cold winter mornings.

slides.title: How We Change With Seasons
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Niti look at their calendars and notice: they play cricket outdoors in winter and autumn, swim in summer, and stay indoors more during monsoon. Our lives change with seasons! says Niti. Gardener Uncle smiles: Yes! Everything changes - what we eat, what we wear, how we play, what grows in farms.

points.text: We wear different clothes in each season - heavy clothes in winter, light in summer
We eat different foods by season - mangoes in summer, oranges in winter, rice crops after monsoon
We play different games - flying kites in autumn, swimming in summer
Festivals happen at certain times - Holi in spring, Diwali in autumn

slides.inSimpleWords: Every season brings changes to clothes, food, games, and celebrations.

image.alt: How We Change With Seasons — Seasons

slides.title: What Plants and Animals Do in Each Season
slides.storyContext: Gardener Uncle shows Arjun and Niti around the garden. In spring, flowers bloom. In summer, fruit trees have mangoes and berries. In autumn, leaves fall. In winter, many trees stand bare. Look at the birds, he says, pointing. Some fly away when it gets cold and come back when it gets warm again. This is called migration.

points.text: In spring and monsoon, plants grow leaves, flowers, and fruits
In autumn and winter, many plants lose their leaves and rest
Some animals, like birds, travel (migrate) to warmer places in winter
Other animals stay and grow thick fur to keep warm in winter

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants and animals change their behavior with each season to stay safe.

image.alt: What Plants and Animals Do in Each Season — Seasons

slides.title: The Migrating Birds
slides.storyContext: In late autumn, Arjun sees huge flocks of birds flying high in the sky, heading south. Where are they going? he asks. To find warmth and food, explains Gardener Uncle. When winter comes, there is not much food here, so birds fly to warmer countries. When spring comes again, they will come back. It is like they are playing a game with the seasons.
slides.inSimpleWords: Many birds travel to warmer places in winter and come back in spring.

slides.title: How Seasons Affect Farming
slides.storyContext: Arjun's grandfather is a farmer. He tells Arjun: A farmer's year is ruled by seasons. In monsoon, I plant. In autumn and winter, crops grow. In early summer, I harvest before the heat gets too strong. Each season has its job.

points.text: Monsoon (June-Sept): Perfect time to plant seeds because of rain
Autumn (Sept-Nov): Crops grow strong, weather is good for farming
Winter (Dec-Feb): Harvesting time - crops are ready, weather is cool
Summer (March-May): Time to rest fields, prepare for next monsoon

slides.inSimpleWords: Farmers follow the seasons - plant in monsoon, harvest in winter.

slides.title: Seasons in India: A Year-Long Journey
slides.storyContext: Arjun draws a circle divided into 4 parts - one for each season. He writes the months and draws pictures of what happens in his town each season.

example.problem: Draw a circle and divide it into 4 parts for the 4 seasons. For each season, write the months and draw: (1) the weather, (2) what people wear, (3) what plants do.
example.solution: SUMMER (Mar-May): Hot, sunny. Light clothes, hats. Trees have leaves, flowers fade. MONSOON (Jun-Sep): Rainy, wet, cool. Raincoats, umbrellas. Green everywhere, crops grow. AUTUMN (Sep-Nov): Cool, dry, pleasant. Normal clothes. Leaves fall, harvest happens. WINTER (Dec-Feb): Cold. Warm clothes, sweaters. Bare trees, some places have frost.

slides.title: My Season Diary
slides.storyContext: Gardener Uncle gives Arjun and Niti a challenge: Watch your town for one month. Write or draw what you see changing every week. Send me a picture by the end of the month.

example.problem: Keep a diary for one month. Each week, draw or write: (1) What is the weather like? (2) What are people wearing? (3) What are plants and trees doing?
example.solution: Week 1: Cloudy, warm. People wear light shirts. Trees have green leaves. Week 2: Hot and sunny. People wear shorts. Flowers are opening. Week 3: Very hot. People stay indoors in afternoon. Plants need watering. Week 4: Evening winds, cooler. Some people wear light shawls. Plants slow growth.

slides.title: Predict the Season
slides.storyContext: Gardener Uncle plays a guessing game with the kids. He describes weather and activities without saying the season name. I am cold and dark. My leaves have fallen. The harvest is done. What season am I?

example.problem: Guess the season based on these clues: (1) Everyone is sweating and the sun feels very strong. (2) Plants need lots of water. (3) People wear light clothes.
example.solution: That is SUMMER! All clues point to summer: high temperatures, bright sun, thirst, light clothing, plants need watering.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can identify seasons by weather, clothing, and what nature is doing.

slides.title: Arjun's Festival Calendar
slides.storyContext: Arjun realizes that many Indian festivals follow the seasons. Holi comes in spring (March) when new crops are ready. Diwali comes in autumn (October-November) after harvest. Pongal/Makar Sankranti come in winter (January) to celebrate harvest. Festivals celebrate what is happening in nature, he exclaims.
slides.inSimpleWords: Indian festivals match the seasons and celebrate harvests and changes.

slides.title: Temperature and Seasons
slides.storyContext: Gardener Uncle brings a thermometer to show Arjun and Niti how temperature changes through the year. In summer, the thermometer might say 45 degrees Celsius - that is very hot! In winter, it might be 10 degrees - that is very cold.

points.text: Temperature is how hot or cold something is - we measure it in degrees Celsius
Summer: 35-45C (very hot) - need light clothes, lots of water
Monsoon: 25-30C (warm but wet) - humidity makes it feel hotter
Winter: 5-20C (cold) - need sweaters and warm clothes

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature measures how hot or cold it is - it changes with seasons.

slides.title: Reading a Thermometer
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns to read a thermometer. The red liquid goes up when it is hot and down when it is cold. Over the year, he tracks the temperature changes and sees the pattern of seasons.

example.problem: If a thermometer shows 40 degrees Celsius, what season is it probably?
example.solution: It is probably summer - 40 degrees is very hot. In winter, temperatures are around 10-15 degrees. In autumn and spring, they are around 25-30 degrees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Thermometers help us know if it is hot (summer) or cold (winter).

slides.title: Niti's Year-Long Observation
slides.storyContext: Niti keeps a detailed journal for the entire year. She records: temperature, rainfall, clothes people wear, festivals, crops being planted and harvested, bird arrivals and departures, tree changes. By the end of the year, her notebook is full of patterns and observations about seasons.
slides.inSimpleWords: Recording observations throughout the year shows how seasons change everything.

slides.title: How Humans Adapt to Seasons
slides.storyContext: Gardener Uncle shows Arjun and Niti how humans in India have adapted to seasons over thousands of years. We build houses to stay cool in summer and warm in winter. We eat seasonal fruits and vegetables. We wear clothes for each season.

points.text: We grow and eat seasonal foods - mangoes in summer, oranges in winter
We design houses to stay cool or warm depending on climate
We have seasonal festivals and celebrations tied to harvests
We plan activities and work around seasonal weather patterns

slides.inSimpleWords: Humans have learned to live with seasons by adapting clothes, food, and homes.

slides.title: Arjun's Seasonal Food Discovery
slides.storyContext: Throughout the year, Arjun notices different fruits and vegetables appear in the market at different times. Mangoes in summer, grapes in monsoon, guavas in autumn, oranges in winter. His grandmother says: Nature gives us exactly what we need in each season. Hot fruits like mangoes cool us in hot summer. Warm fruits help us stay healthy in cold winter.
slides.inSimpleWords: Each season brings different foods that help our bodies stay healthy.

slides.title: Seasonal Food and Health
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns which foods are available in each season and why they are good for our health.

example.problem: What fruits grow in each season in India?
example.solution: SUMMER: Mangoes, watermelon, grapes, berries - water-rich fruits to cool you. MONSOON: Guava, plum, passion fruit - fruits that grow in rains. AUTUMN: Pomegranate, apple, pear - sweet fruits for energy. WINTER: Orange, strawberry, papaya - vitamin-rich fruits for health.

slides.inSimpleWords: Seasonal fruits and vegetables are nature's way of giving us healthy food.

slides.title: Design Your Seasonal Calendar
slides.storyContext: Gardener Uncle gives Arjun and Niti a final challenge: Design a calendar for the whole year showing: (1) seasons, (2) months, (3) weather, (4) festivals, (5) crops, (6) clothes to wear, (7) activities to do.

example.problem: Create a full-year seasonal calendar for your town.
example.solution: Make 4 pages or sections, one for each season. In each section, draw/write: Month, Temperature range, Clothes to wear, Festivals celebrated, Crops grown/harvested, Activities possible, Foods available, Weather patterns.

slides.inSimpleWords: A seasonal calendar shows everything that changes through the year.

slides.title: All About Seasons
slides.storyContext: At the end of the year, Arjun and Niti celebrate the completion of their season's journey. They now understand why the world around them keeps changing.

points.text: There are 4 seasons: Summer (hot), Monsoon (rainy), Autumn (cool), Winter (cold)
Each season has different weather and brings different changes
We change our clothes, food, and activities with each season
Plants grow and rest depending on the season
Seasons happen because of changes in the sun's position and how much heat reaches Earth
Farmers depend on seasons to plant and harvest crops
Indian festivals celebrate seasonal changes and harvests

slides.inSimpleWords: Four seasons bring different weather and changes to nature, plants, and our lives.
